div.h1: 8 GPUs, one process group, two parallelism schemes
div.p: RayResourcePool(process_on_nodes=[8]) — verl.py:185 — creates 8 Ray workers, one per GPU. Each worker is BOTH a training shard AND part of the rollout engine. There is no separate inference cluster: generation and training are colocated on the same cards, which is why the memory budget has to be split statically.
Each weight matrix is split across all 8 cards. Every GPU participates in every token; layers all-reduce between cards. One logical vLLM engine.

ul.li: pro: a 32B that fits on no single card fits comfortably
con: communication-bound, and all 8 cards are busy on one rollout — there is no data-parallel rollout to overlap with

div.p: rollout.mode=async (verl.py:146), served via LLMServerManager (verl.py:196). max_model_len = prompt_length + response_length = 4096 + 8192 = 12288 (verl.py:151) — this is what the KV cache must be sized for.
Parameters, gradients and optimizer state are sharded across the 8 ranks; each rank sees different data and all-gathers the shard it needs per layer.

LoRA rank 32 (save_lora_only=True, verl.py:128) means only the adapter gets gradients and optimizer state — the 64 GB base is frozen. So training memory is dominated by activations, not optimizer state. That is why observed reserved memory (28–39 GB) sits far under the 78.7 GB budget.

div.h2: Why batch size costs time, not memory
div.p: verl packs sequences into micro-batches up to 16384 tokens per GPU rather than a fixed sequence count. Raising batch_size produces MORE micro-batches at the same peak memory — it buys wall-clock, not OOM.

use_remove_padding=True (verl.py:135): sequences are concatenated without padding, so no FLOPs are spent on pad tokens. This needs flash-attn's varlen kernels — which is why provisioning builds flash-attn from source at all.

After each optimizer step the updated LoRA weights are pushed from the FSDP ranks into the vLLM engine so the next rollout samples from the current policy. rollout.checkpoint_engine.backend=naive (verl.py:154).
This is also why kl/policy_vs_ref_k1 ~= 0.001 is the health check that matters: if trainer and sampler ever disagree about the weights, the PPO ratio anchor is silently wrong.

div.h2: The constraint we learned the hard way

pre.code: ValueError: No available memory for the cache blocks

div.p: rollout_tp defaults to 1 (verl.py:50). With tp=1 each vLLM worker tries to hold the whole 64 GB model inside a 0.45 x 143 = 64.4 GB budget, leaving ~0 for KV cache.
Rule: weights_bytes / rollout_tp must leave room for a KV cache big enough for max_model_len x concurrent sequences, inside gpu_memory_utilization x card.

div.h2: Constraints to carry into future experiments

ol.li: Colocation forces a static memory split. Generation and training share each card; gpu_memory_utilization is the dial and it cannot adapt at runtime. Too high starves training, too low starves the KV cache.

TP=8 means the rollout cannot be data-parallel. All 8 cards serve one engine. To overlap rollouts you would need a smaller TP and multiple engines — but TP must stay large enough for the weights to fit.

CPU RAM is not free: 275 GB resident (loss/perf/cpu_memory_used_gb) against a 234 GB cgroup limit on the earlier 1-GPU box. Pod RAM is a real constraint, and free/nproc report the HOST, not the cgroup.
loss/mfu reads 0.00 — model-FLOPs-utilisation is not being computed, so we currently have no direct measure of how well the GPUs are used. Worth wiring up before optimising the training half.

div.h2: Per H200 (143 GB), the static split
div.p: 32B bf16 = 64 GB of weights total, so 8 GB per card once sharded. That is the whole reason rollout_tp: 8 is mandatory — see the crash box.
